system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 6 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 50-70 turns.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: Mr. ___, a man with HCV-related cirrhosis, hepatocellular carcinoma, and a history of TIPS placement, was readmitted for coffee ground emesis and abdominal distension five days after a prior discharge for a similar episode. His hemoglobin was 8.1 g/dL, and he had a positive stool for blood. He underwent an EGD which showed esophagitis and portal hypertensive gastropathy without varices. He received one unit of packed red blood cells and was treated with pantoprazole, octreotide, and ceftriaxone, later transitioned to oral ciprofloxacin. A 6-liter therapeutic paracentesis was performed with albumin administration, and peritoneal fluid analysis showed no infection. His aspirin was held due to recurrent GI bleeding, and pravastatin was increased to 40 mg daily. He improved clinically, with resolution of symptoms and stable labs, and was discharged home with plans for close outpatient follow-up, continuation of liver-directed medications, and monitoring for transplant eligibility.
problems: Other diseases of stomach and duodenum
Unspecified viral hepatitis C without hepatic coma
Atherosclerotic heart disease of native coronary artery without angina pectoris

EXAMINATION:  CHEST (PORTABLE AP)

INDICATION:  ___ year old man with decompensated cirrhosis here with upper GI
bleed, shortness of breath, cough

TECHNIQUE:  Upright AP view of the chest

COMPARISON:  Chest radiograph ___

FINDINGS: 

Patient is status post median sternotomy and CABG.  The heart size is normal. 
The mediastinal and hilar contours are unchanged.  Low lung volumes are
present.  There is crowding of bronchovascular structures with mild pulmonary
vascular congestion.  New small right pleural effusion appears decreased in
size compared to the prior study.  Patchy opacities in the lung bases, more
pronounced on the right, are not substantially changed in the interval, and
likely reflect areas of atelectasis.  Infection or aspiration in the right
lung base however cannot be completely excluded.  No pneumothorax is detected.
Radiopaque focus projects over the right dome of the liver, perhaps a coil,
unchanged.

IMPRESSION: 

Small right pleural effusion, decreased in size from the prior study, with
mild pulmonary vascular congestion.  Patchy opacities in the lung bases may
reflect atelectasis, but aspiration or infection cannot be completely excluded
in the right lung base.

EXAMINATION:  LIVER OR GALLBLADDER US (SINGLE ORGAN)

INDICATION:   ___ with cirrhosis hematemesis  // RUQ thrombosis?

TECHNIQUE:  Grey scale, color, and spectral Doppler ultrasound images of the
abdomen were obtained.

COMPARISON:  Abdominal ultrasound ___

FINDINGS: 

The liver appears diffusely coarsened and nodular consistent with known
cirrhosis.  No focal liver lesions are identified. There is a large amount of
ascites.  Spleen is enlarged, measuring up to 16.4 cm.  There is no
intrahepatic biliary dilation.

The main portal vein is patent with hepatopetal flow.
The TIPS is patent and demonstrates wall-to-wall flow.
Portal vein and intra-TIPS velocities are as follows:
Main portal vein: 29 cm/sec, previously 33 cm/sec
Proximal TIPS: 291 cm/sec, previously 100cm/sec
Mid TIPS: 356 cm/sec, previously 183 cm/sec
Distal TIPS: 200  cm/sec, previously 192 cm/sec

Flow within the left portal vein is away from the TIPS shunt, unchanged from
the prior study. Flow within the right anterior and right posterior portal
vein is  towards the TIPS.

RETROPERITONEUM: Visualized portions of aorta and IVC are within normal
limits.

IMPRESSION:


1. Patent TIPS, although with elevated velocities in the proximal and mid
TIPS.
2. Flow within the left portal vein is away from the TIPS shunt, unchanged.
3. Splenomegaly and large volume ascites.

EXAMINATION:  Ultrasound-guided diagnostic and therapeutic paracentesis

INDICATION:  ___ man with cirrhosis and ascites presenting for
dx/therapeutic paracentesis with IV albumin.

TECHNIQUE:  Ultrasound-guided diagnostic and therapeutic paracentesis

FINDINGS: 

Limited grayscale ultrasound imaging of the abdomen demonstrated a large
amount of ascites. A suitable target in the deepest pocket in the right lower
quadrant was selected for paracentesis.

PROCEDURE:  The procedure, risks, benefits and alternatives were discussed
with the patient and written informed consent was obtained.

A pre-procedure time-out was performed discussing the planned procedure,
confirming the patient's identity with 3 identifiers, and reviewing a
checklist per ___ protocol.

Under ultrasound guidance, an entrance site was selected and the skin was
prepped and draped in the usual sterile fashion. 1% lidocaine was instilled
for local anesthesia.

A 5 ___ catheter was advanced into the largest fluid pocket in the right
lower quadrant and 7 L of clear, straw colored fluid was removed. Fluid
samples were submitted to the laboratory for cell count, differential, and
culture.

The patient tolerated the procedure well without immediate complication.
Estimated blood loss was minimal.

Dr. ___ personally supervised the trainee during the key components
of the procedure and reviewed and agrees with the trainee's findings.

IMPRESSION: 

Technically successful ultrasound-guided diagnostic and therapeutic
paracentesis (7L, RLQ).
Hematology, chemistry, and microbiology samples sent and results are pending.

INDICATION:  ___ year old man with cirrhosis s/p TIPS with ongoing ascites and
GI bleeding from portal gastropathy // assess TIPS patency and dilate if any
TIPS dysfunction. Please leave central line in as patient has poor access.

COMPARISON:  MRI liver ___

TECHNIQUE:  OPERATORS: Dr. ___ and Dr.
___ radiologist performed the procedure. Dr. ___
supervised the trainee during the key components of the procedure and has
reviewed and agrees with the trainee's findings.
ANESTHESIA: Moderate sedation was provided by administrating divided doses of
175mcg of fentanyl and 2.5 mg of midazolam throughout the total intra-service
time of 2 hours 25 minutes during which the patient's hemodynamic parameters
were continuously monitored by an independent trained radiology nurse. 1%
lidocaine was injected in the skin and subcutaneous tissues overlying the
access site.
MEDICATIONS: 175 mcg fentanyl, 2.5 mg versed, 1% lidocaine. Ethanol and STS.
CONTRAST: 163 ml of Optiray contrast.
FLUOROSCOPY TIME AND DOSE: 47.7 min, 533 mGy

PROCEDURE:
1. Right internal jugular venous access using ultrasound.
2. Preprocedure right atrial and splenic vein pressure measurements.
3. Portal venogram.
4. Gastric varix 1 venogram.
5. Ethanol sclerosis and coil embolization of gastric varix 1 and post
embolization venogram.
6. Gastric varix 2 venogram.
7. Ethanol sclerosis, STS sclerosis, and coil embolization of gastric varix 2
and post embolization venogram.
8. Balloon plasty of the TIPS stent to 7 mm.
9. Postprocedure right atrial and splenic vein pressure measurements.
10. Postprocedure portal venogram.

PROCEDURE DETAILS: Following the discussion of the risks, benefits and
alternatives to the procedure, written informed consent was obtained from the
patient. The patient was then brought to the angiography suite and placed
supine on the exam table. A pre-procedure time-out was performed per ___
protocol. The neck was prepped and draped in the usual sterile fashion.

Under continuous ultrasound guidance, the patent right internal jugular vein
was compressible and accessed using a micropuncture needle. Images of
ultrasound access were stored on PACS. Subsequently a Nitinol wire was passed
into the right atrium using fluoroscopic guidance. A small incision was made
at the needle entry site. The needle was exchanged for a micropuncture sheath.
The Nitinol wire was removed and a ___ wire was advanced distally into
the IVC.

The micropuncture sheath was then removed and a 5 ___ x 25 cm sheath was
advanced over the wire into the right atrium.  A pressure measurement was
obtained.  Using an MPA catheter, ___ wire was advanced through the TIPS
stent in into the SMV.  The MPA catheter was then used to advance a Glidewire
into the splenic vein. The catheter was advanced over the wire. The wire was
removed and pressure measurements were obtained in the splenic vein.

The MPA catheter was then exchanged for a straight flush catheter over the
___ wire. The wire was removed and a contrast injection was performed to
confirm positioning. A splenic and portal venogram was performed.

The straight flush catheter was exchanged for an angled glide catheter, which
was used to select gastric varix 1.  The catheter was advanced deeper into the
varix over a Glidewire.  The wire was removed and a contrast injection was
performed to confirm positioning. A gastric varix 1 venogram was performed.

The volume of contrast required to opacify the varix was determined by a
gentle contrast injection.  After flushing the catheter, the equivalent amount
of ethanol was used to sclerosis the varix.  This was followed by placement of
a non detached 0.035 inch coil (3 mm x 4 mm) into gastric varix 1.  An ___
micro catheter preloaded with a Transcend wire was used to cannulate gastric
varix 1 beyond the coil pack.  Additional ethanol sclerosis was performed of
gastric varix 1.  This was followed by a contrast injection into the varix,
which determined stasis and sclerosis of the varix.

The micro catheter was removed.  The angled glide catheter was then attempted
to be used to cannulate gastric varix 2.  Multiple attempts were unsuccessful.
The 5 ___ sheath was exchanged for a 6 ___ ___ 1 sheath over ___
wire.  The angled glide catheter was then able to be directed into gastric
varix 2.  A contrast injection was performed to confirm positioning. A gastric
varix 2 venogram was performed.

The volume of contrast required to opacify the varix was determined by a
gentle contrast injection. After flushing the catheter, the equivalent amount
of ethanol was used to sclerosis the varix. This was followed by placement of
nondetachable 0.018 inch Hilal coils (3 mm x 4 mm (x4)) into gastric varix 2. 
The micro catheter preloaded with a Transcend micro wire was advanced beyond
the coil pack.  Additional sclerosis with STS was performed of gastric varix
2.  A post sclerosis and post embolization venogram was performed, determining
stasis and sclerosis.

The micro catheter was removed.  A ___ wire was advanced into the splenic
vein, and balloon plasty of the TIPS was performed to 7 mm.  The balloon was
removed, and a straight flush catheter was advanced into the splenic vein. The
wire was removed and a contrast injection was performed to confirm
positioning. A post plasty and post gastric varix embolization splenic and
portal venogram was performed.

A straight flush catheter was advanced over the wire into the splenic vein.
The ___ sheath was withdrawn into the right atrium. A splenic vein pressure
measurement was obtained.  The catheter was then withdrawn into the right
atrium and a right atrial pressure was obtained.

The sheath was left in place for a right IJ central line placement, described
in a separate dictation.

The patient tolerated the procedure well. There were no immediate
post-procedure complications.

FINDINGS:


1. Pre procedure right atrial pressure of 5 and splenic vein pressure
measurement of 25 resulting in a portosystemic gradient of 20 mmHg.
2. Contrast enhanced portal venogram showing two gastric varices feeding large
esophageal varices.
3. Gastric varix 1 venogram demonstrating filling of a large esophageal varix.
4. Ethanol sclerosis and coil embolization of gastric varix 1 and post
embolization venogram demonstrating occlusion and sclerosis of the varix with
no further filling of the large esophageal varix.
5. Gastric varix 2 venogram demonstrating filling of gastric varices.
6. Ethanol sclerosis, STS sclerosis, and coil embolization of gastric varix 2
and post embolization venogram demonstrating occlusion and sclerosis of the
varix with no further filling of the varices.
7. Balloon plasty of the TIPS stent to 7 mm.
8. Post procedure portal venogram demonstrates no further filling of gastric
and esophageal varices.
9. Post-procedure right atrial pressure of 13 and portal pressure of 26
resulting in portosystemic gradient of 13 mmHg.

IMPRESSION:


1. Two gastric varices feeding large esophageal varices treated with sclerosis
and embolization with occlusion of the varices and no further filling on post
procedure venograms.
2. Elevated portosystemic gradient of 20 mm Hg, which was reduced to 13 mm Hg
after balloon plasty of the TIPS stent to 7 mm.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. ___, I’m Dr. ___. You’ve been admitted because of the coffee ground vomiting and black stools. We’re concerned about a GI bleed. How are you feeling right now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m feeling okay now. The vomiting stopped after I got to the ER. But my belly’s been really swollen, and I’ve been short of breath.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your abdomen is quite distended. That’s from fluid buildup—ascites—related to your liver disease. We’ll need to drain some of that fluid to help you breathe better and check for infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had that done before. Is it safe again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s safe. We’ll use ultrasound to guide it. We’ll remove some fluid for testing and more to relieve pressure. You’ll get albumin afterward to help your body handle the fluid shift.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And the bleeding? Is it from my varices again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your recent EGD didn’t show active varices. The bleeding is likely from portal hypertensive gastropathy or esophagitis. We’ve started you on pantoprazole and octreotide to reduce pressure and acid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember that drip from last time. Will I need another scope?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. Since you had one recently, we’ll hold off unless symptoms return. We’re watching your hemoglobin closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My sodium was low last time too. Is it bad again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s 132, which is low but stable. We’ll keep you on fluid restriction and monitor it. It’s common with advanced liver disease.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. We did a paracentesis yesterday. Seven liters came out. The fluid didn’t show infection, which is great.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Seven liters? That’s a lot. I do feel a bit better breathing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It is a lot. We’ll keep monitoring your abdomen. We also started ciprofloxacin to prevent infection, given your history of SBP.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on that before. Is it long-term?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we recommend continuing it at home to reduce infection risk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs are stable. The ultrasound showed your TIPS is open, but blood flow is faster than normal. That might explain why you’re still having ascites and bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can that be fixed?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’re planning a procedure to dilate the TIPS and reduce the pressure. That should help with both the fluid and bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it be risky?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a standard procedure for patients like you. There’s a small risk of worsening encephalopathy, but we’ll monitor closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We reviewed your chest X-ray. There’s a small pleural effusion, but it’s improved. Your shortness of breath should get better as we manage the fluid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been using my inhalers. Is the wheezing related to my liver?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not directly, but your history of smoking and low lung function mean we need to manage it carefully. Keep using tiotropium and albuterol as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Before your procedure, I want to confirm: we’ll go in through your neck vein, check the TIPS pressure, dilate it, and treat any abnormal veins causing bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And they’ll numb me?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’ll get sedation and local numbing. You’ll be drowsy but comfortable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The procedure went well. We dilated the TIPS, and the pressure dropped from 20 to 13. We also treated two gastric varices that were likely contributing to the bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good news. Does that mean I’ll stop needing fluid removal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We hope so. It may reduce how often you need paracentesis, but we’ll have to see over time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did another paracentesis yesterday—4 liters. You’re tolerating it well. Your breathing should keep improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel lighter. Any word on my sodium?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It dipped to 123 but you had no symptoms. It’s back to 127 now. We’ll keep monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My wife and I have been thinking—we’d like to talk to palliative care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good idea. They can help with symptom management and planning. I’ll arrange a consult.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Palliative care met with you. They’ll support you at home with comfort and coordination.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. What about my diabetes meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We held your glipizide. You’re on Lantus at 16 units now—down from 33. Monitor your sugars closely and call if they’re over 350.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my aspirin? I know I stopped it last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re still holding it due to the bleeding risk. But given your heart history, we’ll discuss restarting it with your primary team when you’re stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’re planning to discharge you today. Your bleeding has stopped, and your labs are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What meds will I be on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Same as before, except we’re adding sucralfate twice a day for six weeks to help heal your esophagitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the ciprofloxacin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, continue that daily. It’s important for infection prevention.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When should I see my doctor?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Within 10 days for blood work. Call if you have fever, belly pain, confusion, or any signs of bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the palliative care number?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you were given the number. Please call to set up an appointment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doctor. I appreciate everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up if needed.

summary.summary_paragraph: Mr. ___, a man with HCV-related cirrhosis, portal hypertension, and a history of TIPS placement, was admitted for coffee ground emesis and melena, concerning for upper GI bleeding. His symptoms resolved, and recent endoscopic findings suggested portal hypertensive gastropathy and esophagitis as likely sources. He underwent a TIPS revision with balloon dilation, reducing the portosystemic gradient from 20 to 13 mmHg, and sclerotherapy of gastric varices. Two therapeutic paracenteses removed 7L and 4L of fluid, with no evidence of infection. He was managed with octreotide, pantoprazole, and ciprofloxacin prophylaxis. Hyponatremia was monitored and remained stable. His insulin was adjusted, and glipizide was held. Palliative care was consulted per patient request. He improved clinically, with stable vital signs and labs, and was discharged home with follow-up plans, medication adjustments, and recommendations to restart aspirin when bleeding risk decreases.
